questiontext.text: In the test-double taxonomy, a dummy object is one that is:

answer.text: Passed to satisfy a required parameter but never actually called or used

feedback.text: Correct — a dummy only fills a required slot in the interface; the code path under test never invokes it.

answer.text: Programmed to return canned answers to the calls it receives

feedback.text: That describes a stub; a dummy is never actually called.

answer.text: A lightweight but fully working implementation of the dependency

feedback.text: That describes a fake; a dummy has no working behaviour and is never used.

answer.text: Pre-programmed with expectations that fail the test if they are not met

feedback.text: That describes a mock; a dummy verifies nothing.

generalfeedback.text: A dummy is passed only to satisfy a required parameter and is never actually called or used during the code path being tested. It is the simplest double: pure filler.

questiontext.text: A stub is a test double that:

answer.text: Provides canned answers to calls, replacing a real dependency for testing

feedback.text: Correct — a stub returns pre-arranged, fixed values so the SUT can be tested without the real system.

answer.text: Is passed in but never actually called during the test

feedback.text: That describes a dummy; a stub is called and returns canned values.

answer.text: Wraps the real object and records every interaction with it

feedback.text: That describes a spy; a stub does not wrap a real implementation.

answer.text: Fails the test automatically if the expected calls are not made

feedback.text: That describes a mock; a stub performs no verification of its own.

generalfeedback.text: A stub provides canned answers to the calls it receives, standing in for a real dependency so the SUT sees controlled return values. It supports state verification, not behaviour verification.

questiontext.text: A fake is a test double that:

answer.text: Has a real working implementation but takes shortcuts unsuitable for production

feedback.text: Correct — a fake really works (e.g. an in-memory database) but is simplified in ways that make it inappropriate for production.

answer.text: Returns a single fixed canned value and has no internal logic

feedback.text: That describes a stub; a fake has genuine working logic that maintains state across calls.

answer.text: Is never called during the test

feedback.text: That describes a dummy; a fake is a working implementation the SUT actually uses.

answer.text: Is pre-programmed with expectations and verifies them after the test

feedback.text: That describes a mock; a fake verifies nothing — it just works.

generalfeedback.text: A fake has a real, working implementation but takes shortcuts (such as storing data in memory instead of a real database) that make it unsuitable for production. The in-memory user repository and in-memory cache are classic fakes.

questiontext.text: A mock is a test double that:

answer.text: Is pre-programmed with expectations and fails the test if the calls it receives do not match them

feedback.text: Correct — a mock carries expectations about which calls should happen with which arguments, and verifies them.

answer.text: Only returns canned values and never checks how it was called

feedback.text: That describes a stub; a mock actively verifies the interactions.

answer.text: Is a working in-memory implementation of the dependency

feedback.text: That describes a fake; a mock does not provide real working behaviour.

answer.text: Is passed in but never called during the test path

feedback.text: That describes a dummy; a mock exists precisely to check the calls made to it.

generalfeedback.text: A mock is pre-programmed with expectations; if the calls it receives do not match those expectations (right method, right arguments), it fails the test. This is behaviour verification.

questiontext.text: A spy is a test double that:

answer.text: Wraps the real object, calls through to it, and records all interactions

feedback.text: Correct — a spy delegates to the real implementation while recording each call so the test can assert on them afterward.

answer.text: Returns canned values instead of running any real logic

feedback.text: That describes a stub; a spy calls through to the real object, so the real logic still runs.

answer.text: Is passed in but never actually called

feedback.text: That describes a dummy; a spy is used and records every call.

answer.text: Fails the test by itself when its expectations are not met

feedback.text: That describes a mock; a spy only records — the test does the asserting afterward.

generalfeedback.text: A spy wraps the real object, calls through to it (so real behaviour is preserved), and records all interactions. The test then inspects the recorded calls afterward.

questiontext.text: A test passes an object into the SUT only to satisfy a required parameter; the code path under test never invokes any of its methods. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it is never actually called or used; it merely fills a required parameter.
A stub would be called and would return canned values; here nothing is called.
A spy records calls, but here no call is ever made to record.
A mock verifies calls, but here there are no interactions to verify.

generalfeedback.text: When a dependency is required by the API but irrelevant to the test — never invoked on the path under test — the right double is a dummy.

questiontext.text: A double replaces a repository so that findById always returns the fixed record { name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' }, with no real database. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it provides canned answers to calls, replacing the real dependency.
A fake would have real working logic (e.g. store and retrieve many records); this just returns one fixed value.
A mock verifies expected interactions; nothing here checks how the double was called.
A dummy is never called; this double is called and returns a value.

generalfeedback.text: Returning a fixed, pre-arranged value to control what the SUT sees — without a real system — is exactly a stub.

questiontext.text: A double is an in-memory user repository with a real save/findById that store and retrieve records in a Map, avoiding a real database. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it has a real working implementation but takes shortcuts (in-memory storage) unsuitable for production.
A stub returns fixed canned values; this one actually stores and retrieves data with real logic across calls.
A mock verifies expectations; this double provides working behaviour, not verification.
A dummy is never used; this repository is actively used to store and read data.

generalfeedback.text: A working but simplified implementation — such as an in-memory database that really saves and reads records — is a fake.

questiontext.text: A double is set up in advance to expect that send is called with ('alice@example.com', 'Password Reset'); after the SUT runs, calling verify() fails the test if that call did not happen. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it is pre-programmed with expectations and fails the test if the calls do not match.
A stub only returns canned values; it never verifies how it was called.
A fake is a working implementation; it does not carry expectations that fail the test.
A dummy is never called, so it cannot verify any interaction.

generalfeedback.text: Pre-set expectations plus a verification step that fails the test on mismatch is the defining behaviour of a mock.

name.text: Identify the double: wraps and records

questiontext.text: A double wraps the real calculator, calls through to its real add/multiply so results are genuine, and records every call so the test can count them afterward. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it calls through to the real object and records interactions for the test to assert on later.
A stub replaces the real logic with canned values; here the real arithmetic still runs.
A mock fails the test by itself on unmet expectations; this double only records — the test asserts afterward.
A dummy is never called; this double is called and records every call.

generalfeedback.text: Wrapping a real implementation, calling through to it, and recording interactions for later inspection is exactly a spy.

questiontext.text: Which double is characterised by returning fixed values?

feedback.text: Correct — a stub returns fixed, canned values in response to calls.
A dummy returns nothing meaningful because it is never called.
A mock's defining trait is verifying expectations, not merely returning fixed values.
A spy calls through to the real object and records; it does not just return fixed values.

generalfeedback.text: "Returns fixed values" is the signature trait of a stub — it supplies pre-arranged answers so the SUT sees controlled inputs.

questiontext.text: Which double is characterised by verifying expectations?

feedback.text: Correct — a mock verifies that the expected interactions occurred and fails the test otherwise.
A stub returns fixed values and verifies nothing.
A fake is a working implementation; it does not verify expectations.
A dummy is never called, so it verifies nothing.

generalfeedback.text: "Verifies expectations" is the signature trait of a mock: it is pre-programmed with expected calls and fails the test if they are not met.

questiontext.text: Which double is characterised by calling through to the real object and recording interactions?

feedback.text: Correct — a spy calls through to the real implementation and records every interaction.
A stub returns canned values instead of running the real logic.
A mock verifies pre-set expectations; it does not necessarily call through to a real object.
A fake is a separate working implementation, not a wrapper that calls through to the real object.

generalfeedback.text: "Calls through + records" is the signature trait of a spy: it preserves real behaviour while logging the interactions for later assertions.

questiontext.text: A dummy object is never actually called or used during the code path being tested.

feedback.text: Correct — a dummy exists only to satisfy a required parameter; the tested path does not invoke it.
A dummy really is never called; if the SUT invoked it and relied on its return, you would need a stub or another double.

generalfeedback.text: The whole point of a dummy is that it is pure filler: passed to satisfy the interface but never actually called or used on the path under test.

questiontext.text: Which double is best described as having real logic, but simplified (for example, an in-memory cache with genuine TTL eviction but no Redis)?

feedback.text: Correct — a fake has a real working implementation with production-unsuitable shortcuts.
A stub returns fixed values and has no real internal logic.
A mock verifies expectations; it does not provide a simplified working implementation.
A dummy has no behaviour at all and is never called.

generalfeedback.text: "Real logic, simplified" describes a fake — a working implementation (like an in-memory cache with real TTL eviction) that takes shortcuts making it unsuitable for production.

questiontext.text: Your SUT calls a remote weather API for the current temperature. You want to test it with a fixed return value without hitting the network. Which double should you use?

feedback.text: Correct — you need canned return values without a real system, which is a stub.
You are not verifying that a particular call happened; you just need a controlled return value, so a stub is the right fit.
You do not need a whole working weather service, just a fixed value — a stub is simpler and sufficient.
The dependency is actually called and its return value matters, so a dummy will not work.

generalfeedback.text: When you need to control what a dependency returns without running the real system, use a stub — it provides canned answers to the SUT's calls.

questiontext.text: You want to verify that when a user is deleted, an audit-log service is called exactly once with the correct user ID. Which double should you use?

feedback.text: Correct — you must verify a specific interaction with exact arguments, which is behaviour verification, the job of a mock.
A stub only returns canned values; it does not verify that a call was made.
A fake provides working behaviour but does not, by itself, assert that a particular call occurred.
A dummy is never called; it cannot verify an interaction.

generalfeedback.text: When the test must verify that a specific call was made with exact arguments, use a mock — it is pre-programmed with that expectation and fails if it is not met.

name.text: Scenario: working repository without a real DB

questiontext.text: Your SUT needs a database-backed user repository. You want a full working implementation that avoids hitting a real database during unit tests. Which double should you use?

feedback.text: Correct — a fake is a real working implementation (e.g. in-memory) that avoids the real database.
A stub returns fixed values and cannot behave like a real repository across many save/find operations.
A mock verifies interactions; here you need realistic working behaviour, not verification.
A dummy is never used; you need a working repository the SUT actually calls.

generalfeedback.text: When you need realistic but fast behaviour — a working implementation without the real dependency — use a fake, such as an in-memory user repository.

name.text: Scenario: real impl plus call recording

questiontext.text: You want to use the real email-service implementation in your test but also record every call so you can assert on the call counts afterward. Which double should you use?

feedback.text: Correct — a spy wraps the real implementation, calls through to it, and records interactions for later assertions.
A stub replaces the real implementation with canned values; you specifically want the real one to run.
A mock is pre-programmed with expectations and typically replaces the real implementation; here you want the real one to run and to assert afterward.
A dummy is never called and records nothing.

generalfeedback.text: When you want to observe interactions with the real implementation — keeping its behaviour while recording calls — use a spy.

questiontext.text: Your SUT's constructor requires a logger object, but the code path you are testing never actually calls it. Which double should you use?

feedback.text: Correct — the logger is required by the API but irrelevant to the test and never invoked, so a dummy suffices.
A stub is for controlling return values of a called dependency; here the logger is never called, so a dummy is simpler and correct.
A spy records calls, but there are no calls to record on this path.
A mock verifies interactions, but here you are not verifying any interaction with the logger.

generalfeedback.text: When a dependency is required by the API but irrelevant to the test and never invoked, the simplest correct double is a dummy.

questiontext.text: Behaviour verification — asserting that a particular interaction (call) occurred — is the defining purpose of which double?

feedback.text: Correct — a mock exists to verify that expected interactions happened, i.e. behaviour verification.
A stub supports state verification (checking the SUT's resulting value), not behaviour verification.
A fake supports state verification through its working behaviour; it does not verify interactions.
A dummy is never called and verifies nothing.

generalfeedback.text: Behaviour verification checks that the right calls were made. That is exactly what a mock is for; stubs and fakes instead support state verification.

name.text: What kind of verification a stub supports

questiontext.text: A stub that returns a canned value so you can assert on the SUT's resulting output supports which kind of verification?

feedback.text: Correct — you check the SUT's resulting state/return value, not which calls were made.
Behaviour verification checks that calls occurred; a stub does not verify calls — that is a mock's job.

answer.text: Expectation verification that fails the test on mismatch

feedback.text: That is a mock's behaviour, not a stub's; a stub never fails the test on its own.

answer.text: No verification is possible with a stub

feedback.text: The stub enables state verification: you assert on the value the SUT computes from its canned return.

generalfeedback.text: Stubs (and fakes) support state verification: you feed the SUT controlled inputs and assert on its resulting state or return value. Mocks support behaviour verification.

name.text: Match the term: records interactions on a real object

questiontext.text: Which term names a double that wraps a real implementation and records the calls made to it?

feedback.text: Correct — a spy wraps the real object and records interactions.
A mock is pre-programmed with expectations and verifies them itself; it is not defined by wrapping the real object.
A stub replaces the dependency with canned values rather than wrapping the real one.
A fake is a separate working implementation, not a recording wrapper around the real object.

generalfeedback.text: A spy wraps the real object, calls through to it, and records the interactions for later inspection.

name.text: Scenario: in-memory cache with real TTL

questiontext.text: You replace Redis with an in-memory cache that genuinely stores values and evicts them when their TTL expires. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it has real working logic (TTL eviction) but takes shortcuts (in-memory, no Redis) unsuitable for production.
A stub returns fixed values; this cache runs real set/get/eviction logic across calls.
A mock verifies expectations; this double provides working behaviour instead.
A spy wraps and records a real object; this is a standalone working implementation, not a recording wrapper.

generalfeedback.text: A working but simplified implementation with genuine logic (real TTL eviction) and production-unsuitable shortcuts (in-memory) is a fake.

questiontext.text: To test getUserProfile(id, repo), a double's findById always returns { name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' } so you can assert the profile is built correctly. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it supplies a canned return so you can do state verification on the profile the SUT builds.
Nothing here verifies that findById was called a certain way; you only assert on the resulting profile — that is a stub.
A fake would maintain real state; here a single fixed record is returned, which is a stub.
A dummy is never called; this repository is called and returns a value.

generalfeedback.text: Returning a canned record so the test can assert on the SUT's computed output is state verification with a stub.

questiontext.text: A payment double is pre-programmed so that after checkout you can call verify(), which fails unless charge was called with 5000 and 'USD'. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it carries an expectation about the exact call and fails the test if it is not met.
A stub only returns canned values; it does not fail the test based on how it was called.
A spy records calls for the test to assert afterward; here the double itself verifies the expectation via verify(), which is a mock.
A fake is a working implementation; it does not carry expectations that fail the test.

generalfeedback.text: Pre-set expectations about the exact call, checked by the double's own verification step, are the hallmark of a mock.

name.text: Scenario: real math plus call counts

questiontext.text: A calculator double lets computeTotal return the genuine total (40) using the real add/multiply, while also letting the test assert that multiply was called twice. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — the real arithmetic runs (calls through) and every call is recorded for later assertions.
A stub would return canned values, so the real total (40) would not be computed.
A mock would fail by itself on unmet expectations; here the test asserts on recorded calls afterward, which is a spy.
A fake is a substitute implementation; here the real calculator runs and is merely wrapped and recorded — a spy.

generalfeedback.text: Preserving real behaviour while recording calls for later assertions is exactly a spy.

name.text: Scenario: welcome email that only checks result.ok

questiontext.text: To test registerUser, a double's send always returns { ok: true, messageId: 'stub-msg-001' } so the SUT sees the send succeeded, and the test only asserts on the returned registration object — never on how send was called. Which double is this?

feedback.text: Correct — it supplies a canned success response so the SUT can proceed; the test does state verification on the result, not the call.
Nothing here fails the test based on how send was called; only the returned value is asserted, so this is a stub.
A spy would wrap a real email service and record calls; here a canned response replaces the real one, which is a stub.
A dummy is never called; here send is called and its canned return drives the SUT.

generalfeedback.text: Returning a fixed success response so the SUT can continue, then asserting only on the SUT's own output, is a stub supporting state verification.

name.text: Match the term: no calls expected

questiontext.text: Which double has the characteristic no calls expected?

feedback.text: Correct — a dummy is never called; no interactions with it are expected.
A stub is expected to be called and to return canned values.
A mock expects specific calls and verifies them.
A spy expects calls so it can record them.

generalfeedback.text: "No calls expected" is the trait of a dummy: it merely fills a required parameter and is never invoked.

name.text: A stub does not fail the test on its own

questiontext.text: Unlike a mock, a stub never fails the test by itself based on how it was called — it only supplies canned values.

feedback.text: Correct — a stub performs no verification; only a mock is pre-programmed to fail the test when its expectations are not met.
A stub really does no verification; the double that fails the test on unmet expectations is the mock.

generalfeedback.text: Stubs supply canned answers and support state verification; they never fail a test on their own. Failing the test based on the calls received is the mock's behaviour verification.

name.text: Mock used where a stub suffices

questiontext.text: The SUT only needs a dependency's return value to compute a result you then assert on. A colleague writes a mock that also asserts the dependency was called. What is the most appropriate double, and why?

answer.text: A stub — you only need state verification, so asserting on the interaction over-specifies the test and makes it brittle

feedback.text: Correct — when the return value is all that matters, a stub keeps the test focused on the outcome rather than the implementation's call pattern.

answer.text: A mock — always verify every call to be safe

feedback.text: Verifying calls you do not care about couples the test to implementation details and makes it brittle; a stub is the right tool here.

answer.text: A fake — you need a full working implementation

feedback.text: No working implementation is needed; a single canned return (a stub) is enough.

answer.text: A dummy — the dependency is irrelevant

feedback.text: The dependency's return value is actually used, so a dummy will not work; you need a stub.

generalfeedback.text: Using a mock where only the outcome matters is a classic mock/stub misuse: it verifies interactions you do not care about, coupling the test to how the SUT is implemented. Prefer a stub and do state verification.

questiontext.text: A test breaks every time the SUT is refactored — even when its observable output is unchanged — because it asserts on the exact sequence of internal calls. This is a classic symptom of:

answer.text: Over-mocking — behaviour verification of interactions that do not matter couples the test to the implementation

feedback.text: Correct — over-using mocks with strict expectations makes tests brittle against harmless refactors.

answer.text: Under-stubbing — too few canned return values

feedback.text: The problem is not missing return values; it is asserting on internal calls that should not be checked.

answer.text: Using a fake instead of a real database

feedback.text: A fake would not cause breakage on refactors; the cause is strict interaction assertions.

answer.text: Using a dummy that is never called

feedback.text: A dummy causes no assertions at all; over-mocking is the cause of the brittleness.

generalfeedback.text: Over-mocking pins tests to the SUT's internal call structure. When you assert on interactions that do not affect observable behaviour, harmless refactors break the tests. Favour state verification (stubs/fakes) unless the interaction is genuinely the thing under test.

name.text: When a stub is not enough

questiontext.text: The SUT saves a record and later reads it back, expecting consistent state across several calls, and also relies on TTL expiry. A stub returning one fixed value cannot reproduce this. What should you use instead?

answer.text: A fake — a working implementation that maintains state across calls (e.g. in-memory store with real TTL)

feedback.text: Correct — reproducing consistent, stateful behaviour across calls requires a working implementation, i.e. a fake.

answer.text: A mock — verify each save and read call

feedback.text: Verifying calls does not give you the consistent stateful behaviour the SUT depends on; you need a working fake.

answer.text: A dummy — the dependency is irrelevant

feedback.text: The dependency is central to the behaviour; a dummy is never called and cannot store state.

answer.text: More stubs — one canned value per call

feedback.text: Hand-tuning canned values for every call is fragile and cannot model real interactions like TTL expiry; a fake is the proper tool.

generalfeedback.text: When the SUT needs realistic, stateful behaviour across many calls (save/read consistency, TTL expiry), a stub's single canned value is insufficient. A fake — a lightweight working implementation — is the right trade-off.

name.text: How a spy differs from a mock

questiontext.text: Which statement best captures how a spy differs from a mock?

answer.text: A spy calls through to the real object and records interactions for the test to assert on afterward; a mock is pre-programmed with expectations and fails the test itself if they are not met

feedback.text: Correct — the spy records and lets the test verify later; the mock carries and enforces expectations by itself.

answer.text: A spy verifies expectations by itself, whereas a mock only records calls

feedback.text: This reverses them: the mock verifies expectations; the spy records for later assertion.

answer.text: A spy returns only canned values, whereas a mock runs the real implementation

feedback.text: It is the spy that calls through to the real implementation; a stub returns canned values.

answer.text: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable

feedback.text: They differ: recording-for-later (spy) versus pre-set-expectations-that-fail-the-test (mock).

generalfeedback.text: A spy wraps and calls through to the real object, recording calls so the test asserts on them afterward. A mock is pre-programmed with expectations and fails the test by itself when they are not met.

name.text: Borderline: records but does not self-verify

questiontext.text: A double records every call it receives but never fails the test by itself; the test inspects the recorded calls afterward to decide pass/fail. Which double is this, most specifically?

feedback.text: Correct — recording interactions for the test to assert on later, without self-verifying, is a spy.
A mock fails the test itself on unmet expectations; here the double only records and the test decides afterward.
A stub returns canned values; recording calls for later inspection is the spy's role.
A dummy is never called, so it records nothing.

generalfeedback.text: The distinguishing line is who verifies: a spy records and the test asserts afterward; a mock is pre-programmed and fails the test on its own.

questiontext.text: What is the essential difference between a mock and a stub?

answer.text: A mock is pre-programmed with expectations and fails the test if the calls do not match (behaviour verification); a stub only supplies canned values and never fails on its own (state verification)

feedback.text: Correct — mocks verify interactions, stubs supply controlled state.

answer.text: A mock returns canned values while a stub verifies interactions

feedback.text: This reverses them: stubs return canned values, mocks verify interactions.

answer.text: A mock is a working implementation while a stub is never called

feedback.text: A working implementation is a fake, and a never-called double is a dummy — neither is the mock/stub distinction.

answer.text: They are the same; both verify expectations

feedback.text: Only the mock verifies expectations; the stub does not.

generalfeedback.text: Both can supply return values, but only a mock carries expectations and fails the test when the interactions do not match. A stub does no verification — it exists for state verification.

name.text: Replacing a spy with a stub

questiontext.text: A spy wraps the real calculator so computeTotal returns the genuine 40 while recording calls. If you replaced the spy with a stub, what would change?

answer.text: The stub would return canned values, so the real arithmetic would no longer run and the genuine total would not be produced

feedback.text: Correct — a stub replaces the real logic with fixed answers, losing the real behaviour a spy preserves.

answer.text: Nothing — a stub and a spy behave identically

feedback.text: They differ: a spy calls through to the real object; a stub returns canned values instead.

answer.text: The stub would fail the test on unmet expectations

feedback.text: Failing on unmet expectations is a mock's behaviour, not a stub's.

answer.text: The stub would record calls just like the spy

feedback.text: Recording calls is the spy's role; a plain stub does not record for later assertions.

generalfeedback.text: A spy calls through to the real implementation (real math runs) while recording. A stub would substitute canned values, so the genuine computation — and any bug it might reveal — would not run.

questiontext.text: A collaborator simply returns a value and has no side effects that matter to the SUT's contract. Mocking it and asserting it was called leads to:

answer.text: Tests coupled to implementation details, when a stub returning the value would have been simpler and sufficient

feedback.text: Correct — verifying calls to a side-effect-free collaborator adds brittleness without value; a stub is the right choice.

answer.text: Stronger tests, because verifying every call is always better

feedback.text: Verifying calls that do not matter to the contract couples the test to implementation and adds no real assurance.

answer.text: A need for a fake instead

feedback.text: No working implementation is required; a simple stub of the return value is enough.

answer.text: A dummy, since the collaborator is irrelevant

feedback.text: The collaborator's return value is used, so it is not irrelevant; a stub is appropriate.

generalfeedback.text: For a collaborator whose only role is returning a value, a stub supports state verification cleanly. Mocking it verifies interactions that do not matter, coupling the test to implementation and making it brittle.

questiontext.text: A fake in-memory database gives realistic, stateful behaviour in tests. What is a genuine drawback of relying on it?

answer.text: Because it has real logic that takes production-unsuitable shortcuts, the fake itself can contain bugs or diverge from the real dependency's behaviour

feedback.text: Correct — a fake is real code with shortcuts, so it must be maintained and can behave differently from production.

answer.text: It cannot maintain state across calls

feedback.text: Maintaining state across calls is precisely what a fake does well; that is its strength.

answer.text: It verifies interactions and so makes tests brittle

feedback.text: Verification is a mock concern; a fake does not verify interactions.

answer.text: It returns only a single canned value

feedback.text: That describes a stub, not a fake; a fake has genuine working logic.

generalfeedback.text: A fake is a working implementation with shortcuts unsuitable for production. That real logic is itself code: it can harbour bugs and may not match the production dependency, so it carries maintenance and fidelity risk.

questiontext.text: A dependency is required to construct the SUT, but on the path under test it is never invoked at all. Using a stub with canned returns would work but is unnecessary. What is the most specific correct double?

answer.text: Dummy — because nothing is ever called, pure filler is the most specific fit

feedback.text: Correct — with no interaction at all, a dummy is the minimal and most precise choice.

answer.text: Stub — always provide canned returns to be safe

feedback.text: A stub would work but over-specifies: there are no calls needing a return, so a dummy is the most specific fit.

answer.text: Spy — to record that it was not called

feedback.text: There is nothing to record; a spy adds machinery for interactions that never happen.

answer.text: Mock — to verify it is never called

feedback.text: You could verify a no-call expectation, but the scenario only requires filling the parameter, so a dummy is the most specific choice.

generalfeedback.text: When a double is passed only to satisfy a required parameter and is never invoked, the most specific correct choice is a dummy. A stub would function but implies canned returns that are never needed.

name.text: Most specific: must confirm the call happened

questiontext.text: The whole point of a test is to confirm that send was actually called with subject 'Password Reset', and the test must fail if it was not. Which double is the most specific fit?

answer.text: Mock — the requirement is behaviour verification with an exact expected call that fails the test on mismatch

feedback.text: Correct — a mock is pre-programmed with that expectation and fails if the call does not match.

answer.text: Stub — return a canned value and move on

feedback.text: A stub cannot make the test fail based on whether the call happened; that is behaviour verification, a mock's job.
A working implementation does not, by itself, assert that the expected call occurred.

answer.text: Dummy — the email service is irrelevant

feedback.text: The interaction is exactly what the test cares about, so a dummy is wrong.

generalfeedback.text: When confirming that a specific call happened (with exact arguments) is the purpose of the test, use a mock — it verifies the expectation and fails on mismatch.

name.text: How a stub can mask a defect

questiontext.text: A test passes with a stubbed dependency, yet the system fails in production. How can a stub mask a real defect?

answer.text: The stub returns canned values, so the real dependency's (possibly buggy) logic is never exercised in the test

feedback.text: Correct — replacing the real logic with fixed answers means genuine faults in that logic go untested.

answer.text: The stub verifies too many expectations

feedback.text: Stubs verify nothing; masking comes from bypassing the real logic, not from verification.

answer.text: The stub calls through to the real object

feedback.text: Calling through is a spy's behaviour; a stub substitutes canned values, which is what causes the masking.

answer.text: The stub maintains real state across calls

feedback.text: Maintaining real state is a fake's behaviour; a stub returns fixed values and therefore can hide real defects.

generalfeedback.text: Because a stub supplies canned answers instead of running the real dependency, any defect in that dependency's genuine logic is never triggered by the test — so the test can pass while production fails.

questiontext.text: Consider the typical usage order for a mock versus a spy. Which statement is correct?

answer.text: With a mock you set expectations before exercising the SUT and verify after; with a spy you set no expectations up front and only assert on recorded calls afterward

feedback.text: Correct — the mock's expectations are declared first (e.g. expect(...)) and checked after; the spy simply records and is asserted on later.

answer.text: Both require expectations to be declared before the SUT runs

feedback.text: Only the mock declares expectations up front; a spy records without pre-set expectations.

answer.text: A spy declares expectations up front; a mock never does

feedback.text: This reverses them: the mock declares expectations; the spy does not.

answer.text: Neither can be verified after the SUT runs

feedback.text: Both are checked after the SUT runs — the mock via its own verify, the spy via test assertions on recorded calls.

generalfeedback.text: A mock is pre-programmed: expectations are set before the SUT runs and verified afterward. A spy sets no expectations up front — it records calls, and the test asserts on those records after the fact.

name.text: Most specific: real output must run while counting calls

questiontext.text: A test needs the real logger to genuinely produce '[LOG] Processing 5' while also counting how many times log and warn were called. A stub returning canned values would lose the real output. Which double is the most specific fit?

answer.text: Spy — it wraps the real logger, calls through so the genuine output is produced, and records the calls for counting

feedback.text: Correct — needing the real behaviour and a record of the calls is exactly what a spy provides.
Canned returns would discard the real logger's genuine output, which the test specifically requires.

answer.text: Mock — pre-set expectations that fail the test

feedback.text: The test asserts on recorded counts afterward rather than pre-declaring a strict expectation; that is a spy, and a mock would typically replace the real implementation.
A fake is a substitute implementation; here the real logger must run and merely be wrapped and recorded, which is a spy.

generalfeedback.text: When the test needs the real implementation's genuine behaviour preserved and the calls recorded for later counting, the most specific double is a spy: it calls through and records, unlike a stub (canned values) or a mock (pre-set self-verifying expectations).

questiontext.text: A suite asserts on the SUT's output and that every collaborator was called with exact arguments; it breaks on nearly every refactor. What is the best remedy?

answer.text: Prefer state verification with stubs/fakes where possible, and reserve mocks for interactions that genuinely matter (e.g. real side effects)

feedback.text: Correct — reducing needless behaviour verification decouples tests from implementation and cuts brittleness.

answer.text: Add more mocks so every call is verified

feedback.text: More interaction assertions increase coupling and brittleness — the opposite of the fix.
Dummies are never called; the SUT relies on real return values and some genuine interactions, so dummies cannot replace them.

answer.text: Delete the assertions on the SUT's output

feedback.text: The output assertions are the valuable, stable ones; it is the over-verification of interactions that should be trimmed.

generalfeedback.text: Brittleness here comes from over-mocking — verifying interactions that do not matter. Lean on state verification (stubs and fakes) and use mocks only where confirming an interaction (such as a real side effect) is genuinely the point.
